questions.q: New instances take ~1–3 minutes to detect load, boot and warm up. A traffic spike lasts 60 s. What saves you?
choices: A minimum replica count that survives the burst on its own
questions.why: The spike can be over before new instances arrive. Autoscaling handles slow curves (day/night, growth); the floor handles bursts.
questions.note: Autoscaling: the minimum survives bursts, the maximum handles growth

questions.q: A ×3 burst sends 3,300 rps to the service. Each replica does 1,000 rps and you accept ρ ≈ 0.85 for a short burst. Minimum replicas?
questions.why: Usable per replica in a burst = 1,000 × 0.85 = 850 rps. 3,300 ÷ 850 ≈ 3.9, so 4.
questions.note: Autoscaling: the minimum survives bursts, the maximum handles growth

questions.why: ≈ 0.6 keeps waits short all day; ≈ 0.85 is slower but bounded for a minute. At or above 1.0 the queue grows without limit.
questions.note: Autoscaling: the minimum survives bursts, the maximum handles growth

questions.q: Besides bursts, what else must the replica floor cover?
choices: The cache or CDN missing (purge, deploy, outage) and sending traffic straight to the service
questions.why: With a CDN at 90% hits the service sees ~10% of traffic. If the CDN misses, it sees all of it at once.
questions.note: Autoscaling: the minimum survives bursts, the maximum handles growth

questions.q: Which of these does a queue help with?
choices: Redirect GET /{code}, the browser is waiting
Bulk POST /shorten imports, which can be async
questions.why: A queue smooths work that nobody waits on: bulk imports, click events, emails. Anything a user is waiting for still needs capacity now.
questions.note: Spikes on a hot link: CDN, not a queue

questions.q: In the URL shortener with a CDN, a 4-replica service went from 10k to 40k rps. The service hit ρ 1.10. What happened to p99?
choices: It jumped to seconds (~3 s) and kept backing up
questions.why: Above ρ 1.0 more arrives than can be served, so the line grows every second and waits explode.
